title: Free as the wilderness (Numbers Rabbah 1:7)
hook: the Torah was given in the desert, free as fire and water, to whoever makes themselves open
tomorrow: what happens to God's name when nobody bears witness?

segments.voice: Yesterday, one voice at Sinai, and each person heard it according to their own strength, from elders to babies. Each according to strength. Today, the place where that voice spoke.

Some things have no paywall. A public library card. A water fountain in the park. The sunset over a parking lot. Nobody checks your ID at a sunset. The book of Numbers opens with an address: God spoke to Moses "in the wilderness of Sinai." Not a city. Not a palace. Not a temple with a door and a guard. Why there? One question for today: who gets the Torah, and what does it cost?
screen: `NO PAYWALL.` → `IN THE WILDERNESS OF SINAI.` → `WHO GETS IT? WHAT DOES IT COST?`

segments.voice: Numbers Rabbah answers with three things. The Torah came with fire, on a smoking mountain. With water, as clouds poured down. And in the wilderness. All three are free to everyone in the world. So are the words of Torah: free to all who come. Then a second line, the hard one: whoever doesn't make themselves ownerless like the wilderness can't acquire wisdom and Torah. The Hebrew is hefker, land nobody owns. A desert has no gate, no owner, no fence. So the price isn't money. It's openness. That may be why the line is hard: paying for something is often easier than putting down what you already guard. Now a neighbor. In the Gospel of Matthew, when Jesus sends out his disciples, he tells them, in the King James words, "freely ye have received, freely give." Some Christian readers hear in it a charge to share what God gave without charging for it. Shared ground: a gift from God that came free and should stay free. The honest difference: in Matthew, the gift is what the disciples received from Jesus and are sent to pass on. In the midrash, the gift is the Torah itself, and the condition sits on the receiver: be as open as a desert. Each says it in its own words, from its own book, and neither needs the other to be the same.
screen: `FIRE, WATER, WILDERNESS.` · `HEFKER: OWNED BY NO ONE.` · `MATTHEW: FREELY GIVE.` · `THE GIFT, AND WHO MUST OPEN.` · then, large: `FREE AS THE WILDERNESS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let your hands rest loose, shoulders down. Picture open desert in every direction: no fence, no door, no owner. For the rest of the sit, whenever you catch yourself guarding something, a grudge, an opinion, a plan, let that fence come down a little.
screen: `HANDS LOOSE.` · `OPEN DESERT, NO FENCE.` · `LET ONE FENCE COME DOWN.`

howItsDone: Jewish study is traditionally open to any learner who comes, and Jews read Numbers Rabbah's teaching about the wilderness around Shavuot, when the book of Numbers and the giving of the Torah are both in view.
